Now, Sun Wukong’s transformation had some limitations, like I mentioned here, if he transformed into a person or an unusual object, he must keep his tail intact, so it must be disguised.
There were also times he LOL’ed too hard and accidentally broke his transformation.
The most notable example of Wukong using transformation to strengthen himself for battle, was the Three-Head-Six-Arm form.
When he fought Nezha, he mimicked the ability to battle him evenly.
I do believe Sun Wukong particularly liked this form, and had re-used it many times against difficult opponents.

Most of the other times he used his transformation, it was for the purpose of disguise and espionage.A recurring trope in the story was that Wukong often fought his opponent to a draw on the first time (or his opponent fled and never returned).
He would then transform into an animal or lesser demon, and sneak into the enemy lair, where he would discover the demon’s weakness or nemesis.
Then Sun Wukong would challenge the demon a second time, and this time Wukong could soundly defeat, or he would call for help from someone to assist him.
Sun Wukong always knew the importance of intelligence gathering.
However, Sun Wukong would not gain any secret abilities of the person he transformed to, because he will not gain knowledge known only by the real person.
Therefore, his transformation could only match the target’s appearance and physical power, not necessarily in any skill or technique they possessed.
In one chapter where he fought Hong Hai’er, he did his usual intelligence gathering in a rather foolish way.
He transformed into the Ox King (Hong Hai’er’s father), because the Ox King was once an old friend; Wukong thought he could imitate him well.
Hong Hai’er welcomed “father,” but soon became suspicious.
In a conversation, he said he had a meeting with a fortune teller, but couldn’t remember if his date of birth is correct.
So he asked “father” to give him an answer.
When Wukong was unable to answer, Hong Hai’er immediately called out his disguise and attacked, but Wukong escaped and had the last laugh over trolling Hong Hai’er into calling him father.
I gotta say, Hong Hai'er was definitely one of the upper tier opponents that Sun Wukong faced.
Not only did he critically injure Wukong once, he was smart enough that he knew the modern concept the of security questions.
Wukong tried to hack his account using his dad's fake identity and got caught.

The Nature of Transformation: While Sun Wukong can transform into various beings and objects, these transformations often rely on his own understanding and cunning.
Buddha's nature is fundamentally different; he embodies spiritual power that cannot be replicated or matched through mere physical transformation.
The Limits of Power: Sun Wukong’s transformations are often tied to his ego and confidence.
In the face of Buddha, he realizes that brute strength and cleverness are insufficient.
This encounter serves as a humbling experience, emphasizing that true power lies in wisdom, compassion, and enlightenment rather than just physical prowess.
Narrative Purpose: From a storytelling perspective, this moment illustrates a key turning point for Sun Wukong.

His defeat by Buddha leads to his eventual redemption and growth as a character, aligning with the broader themes of the journey, which include self-discovery, humility, and the pursuit of enlightenment.

In summary, Sun Wukong's failure to effectively use his transformative abilities against Buddha serves to highlight the themes of power, enlightenment, and the limitations of even the most formidable beings when faced with true wisdom.

Sun Wukong is one of the most powerful characters in all classic Chinese novels.
Sun Wukong will never die himself.
When he was young, he learned the skill of longevity from Master Puti.
Then, he ate thousands of Heaven peaches, a single one of which can bring people a lifetime as long as forever.
Plus, he ate tons of Taishang Lord's longevity Dan medicine, and later, ginseng fruits, which are also food for longevity.
More importantly, the Hell could not control him because he broke into the Hell and destroyed his records when he was young.

No one is able to kill Sun Wukong.
Many demons on the way to India tried to kill the monkey.
Some of them tried to behead him; some of them tried to kill him in boiling oil; some of them tried the disembowelment; and some of them tried to poison.
However, none of them really killed the monkey.
The monkey has unlimited energy and strength.
He could fight solely against millions of soldiers in either Heaven or Hell, or thousands of demons in a mountain, and finally win the battle.
Usually, he can control the weather, because gods controlling weathers usually obey his orders.
His eye sight is remarkably good.
It is as good as the X ray.
Almost nothing can fool the monkey's eyes, which are often called f iery and golden eyes.
Sun Wukong is fast.
He can move 108,000 li (1 li is about 0.5 km) with one single jump.
This skill is called somersault cloud.
He can freely turn himself into anything he wish, such as a rock, a tree, a man, an eagle, or even the enemy.
This skill is called 72 changes.
He can pluck out his hairs and turn them into anything else, even another Sun Wukong.
Sometimes when the enemy was too strong, Sun Wukong would pluck a hair and crew it, and then turn it into hundreds of smaller Sun Wukongs to help himself.
His weapon, the Golden Cudgel, has a weight of 13,500 jin (about 6.75 tons).
He has friends and allies everywhere.
Many ghosts, spirits, dragons lords, city gods, mountain gods, star gods, as well as many notable Bodhisattva and Arhats and Taoism gods, will come to help him in emergency.
Maybe the only notable weakness of the monkey is his ability to fight in water.
However, he still broke into the Dragon Palace in the East China Sea and defeated Eastern Sea Dragon Lord's army.
Later, this weakness is further remitted, because his two fellow apprentices, Bajie the pig and the sandy monk, are good at fighting under water.
In the novel, only Buddha (Gautama), Guanyin (Avalokitesvara) and very few else have significantly greater powers.
Some other characters, such as Nezha, Er-lang God and the fake Sun Wukong, can rival him, but they cannot defeat the monkey.

I have once compiled a list of Sun Wukong's specific powers and abilities, superhero style.
Ruyi Jingu Bang 如意金箍棒: This is the magical pole that Sun Wukong claimed from the Dragon Palace.
It was extremely heavy and had the power to grow and shrink.
In its original form it was a giant metal pillar, which was why the Dragon King offered it to him, thinking he could not take it.
Sun Wukong used it as a staff, and if he needed to conceal it, he shrunk it and threw it inside his ear.
I have once compiled a list of Sun Wukong's specific powers and abilities, superhero style.
Ruyi Jingu Bang 如意金箍棒: This is the magical pole that Sun Wukong claimed from the Dragon Palace.
It was extremely heavy and had the power to grow and shrink.
In its original form it was a giant metal pillar, which was why the Dragon King offered it to him, thinking he could not take it.
Sun Wukong used it as a staff, and if he needed to conceal it, he shrunk it and threw it inside his ear.
The original owner of the pole was actually The Great Yu, the mythological sage king responsible for cultivating the rivers of the central plains.
He used its powers to measure the depth of water, so basically it was…an ancient magical measuring tape?
Jin Gu 紧箍: Sun Wukong's iconic golden headband.
It was more of a curse than a gift.
It was given to Tang Sanzang by Lady Guanyin.
After Wukong unknowingly put it on, Sanzang could say a magical chant, and it would tighten itself around Wukong's head, giving him intense pain.
It could not be removed, not even by Sanzang.
In the very final scene of the book, Wukong asked about it, and found out it had magically disappeared once he completed his quest and reached enlightenment.
This item was both a plot device/kryptonite that was in place so Sun Wukong had to obey his master, and in a way, a Buddhism metaphor.
Nimbus cloud 筋斗云: Sun Wukong's flying was actually an ability/spell, not an item.
He could flip into the sky and fly 108,000 li in a single bound.
In a lot of adaptations the authors took the statement about him “riding a cloud" too literally, and instead made it an artifact.
In the original story, Wukong stated he could carry the heaviest inanimate objects in flight, but not a mortal; almost like mortals are reversed-Mjolnirs that were encumbered to stay on the Earth.
I do believe Dragon Ball gave a humourous nod to this, by showing us that those with an impure heart (like Roshi) could not ride Nimbus.
Sun Wukong’s armour: This was the armour that Sun Wukong wore in the first arc of the story.
It had a red and gold colour design, and a phoenix tail crown.
He obtained it by effectively extorting the Dragon King, who reluctantly summoned his brothers to give him this set of armour as tribute.
He wore it during the battle against the Heavenly Palace, though it was not likely that they had any special powers.
It was destroyed when he was imprisoned under the mountain by Buddha.
